newsitem.title: USA: Allergy shots fail to cut children's asthma attacks.
newsitem.headline: Allergy shots fail to cut children's asthma attacks.

text.p: The common technique of using allergy shots to help reduce childhood asthma problems has failed to work in a study of 121 children, according to a report in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
But the finding were so unexpected that authors of the report are urging caution in its acceptance, the report said.
Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine researchers gave 60 youngsters placebo shots while 61 others received injections designed to protect them against allergies to several substances.
According to conventional wisdom, the children who were immunised against their allergies should have needed less asthma medicine than those who received the placebo.
But they did not. The study found the amount of medicine consumed by the two groups was essentially the same.
"We were unable to demonstrate any effect of allergen injections on the course of the asthma over a period of 30 months," said the Johns Hopkins team led by Dr. N. Franklin Adkinson Jr.

About one in 20 adults suffer from the shortness of breath caused by periodic attacks of asthma. The disease is far more common in children -- about one in 10 have it -- and many outgrow it. Attacks are often sparked by an allergic reaction to pollen, dust, animal fur, feathers or other substances.
Past research has shown that when a child is sensitive to a single allergen, allergy shots reduce symptoms.

The Hopkins team did not set out to cast doubt on that treatment. They were curious about the effectiveness of allergy shots designed to protect children who were sensitive to several substances. In this case, many of the children were allergic to dust mites, short ragweed and rye-group grasses.
The new findings are expected to force doctors to take a hard look at the treatment and whether it is a waste of time and money.
Adkinson and his colleagues acknowledged that the findings "are contrary to widely held clinical opinion and the results of some studies of asthma and single allergens."
One possible explanation for the unexpected result may be the youngsters were getting too much medicine to start with.

The study was designed to encourage each child's doctor to reduce the amount of medicine prescribed for the youngster whenever tests showed an improvement in the youngster's condition. Often, cautious doctors resisted.
"Nonetheless, over time, medications were withdrawn and the children in both groups did well, as evidenced by the significant declines in medication scores," the researchers said.
They said 34 children (of a total of 121) were taking no medications by the end of the study, indicating that the effort to reduce medications during the study was successful.
The improvement in both groups may have overwhelmed the benefits of the allergy shots, the Adkinson team said.
He noted "the participants in our study were not typical of allergic children treated for asthma in routine clinical practice."
They came from families willing to be involved in a long-term study, the children and parents got in-depth counselling and the youngsters were seen by a doctor every two or three weeks.
As a result, the doctors noted a "substantial" improvement in their asthma even before the children were segregated into treatment and control groups.

All of this, said the Adkins group, "may have controlled the disease process to such an extent that it would have been difficult to show the clinical benefit of any number of relatively weak but nevertheless effective therapies."
